title: The rook
outcomes: Taps every square a rook can reach, including a capture and the squares up to a blocking piece
Works out how far a rook can slide along a row or column before a piece blocks it
Says why a rook cannot reach a square that shares neither its row nor its column

steps.say: Slide the rook to the star. Moves that give check are not offered.
Two slides this time: along a row, then up a column.

steps.text: The rook slides any distance along a **row** or a **column**, and may stop on any square along the way.

steps.say: Your king is in the way. Go round it.

steps.text: The rook cannot jump. Its own piece blocks it. It may take an enemy piece by landing there, but never has to.

steps.say: A star can hold an enemy piece. Take it.

steps.caption: Lit squares are where the rook can go. Its own pawn and the black pawn block it. It may take the black pawn.

claims.statement: From d4 the rook reaches these squares and no others.

steps.say: The star shares no row or column with the rook. Find the way.

steps.caption: The lit square shares neither the rook's row nor its column, and a rook never moves diagonally. One slide cannot reach it.

claims.statement: The rook cannot move from c3 to e5 in one move.
The rook can move up its own column to c5.

steps.prompt: Say it back: how does a rook move, and what stops it?

steps.text: **Model answer.** A rook slides along a row or column, stopping before its own pieces or taking an enemy piece. It never moves diagonally.

steps.say: One last run: take the pawn, then reach the second star.

sources: Rebuilt as a star-grab lesson on 8 Nov 2026 (docs/reach-step.md); wording original.
